overview.heading: Collect every sample safely, cleanly, and only once
overview.intro: Diagnostic results are only as good as the sample they come from. This lesson covers how the clinical team collects blood, urine, fecal, and ear samples: which vein or method to use, how to restrain and prepare the patient, how to handle needles and sharps safely, and which tube each ordered test requires. Getting these right the first time avoids repeat draws, protects the sample from hemolysis and contamination, and keeps both the patient and the team safe.
objectives: Perform and describe jugular, lateral saphenous, and cephalic venipuncture, including restraint, occlusion, and bevel-up needle placement.
Distinguish sterile cystocentesis from a voided free catch sample and explain when each is appropriate.
Collect an ear swab sample and prepare a microscope slide using the rolling technique.
Select needles, syringes, and blood tubes correctly and handle sharps according to OSHA guidance.
Handle and mix samples so results are not compromised by hemolysis or contamination.
overview.connectsForward: Sample collection feeds every other Clinical Diagnostics skill: in-house laboratory workflows, imaging support, and case presentation all depend on correctly collected, correctly labeled, and correctly handled samples.

modules.content:
Blood collection is the first sample-collection skill in Clinical Diagnostics. Watch the full blood draw demonstration, then review the key terms used throughout the rest of this lesson.

Screen 1

Blood Collection / Key Terms in Blood Collection

What to watch for

  • How the restrainer occludes the vessel and stays clear of the needle.
  • Bevel-up needle placement and the flashback of blood in the hub.
  • Removing the needle from the syringe before filling tubes.
  • Pressure on the site, then positive reinforcement for the patient.

Key terms

Key Terms in Blood Collection

Review each term before moving on. These terms are used in the recap and in the end-of-course assessment.

Venipuncture

The procedure of collecting blood from a vein. Includes jugular, lateral saphenous, and cephalic venipuncture.

Jugular Venipuncture

Collecting blood from the jugular vein in the neck.

Lateral Saphenous Venipuncture

Collecting blood from the lateral saphenous vein in the hind leg.

Cephalic Venipuncture

Collecting blood from the cephalic vein in the front leg.

Occlusion

Applying pressure to a blood vessel to temporarily stop or slow blood flow, making the vein more prominent.

Bevel

The slanted opening at the tip of a needle. Should face up during venipuncture for smooth entry.

Anticoagulant

A substance added to blood collection tubes to prevent clotting. Examples include EDTA, lithium heparin, and serum separator.

Hemolysis

The rupture or destruction of red blood cells, which can occur if blood is forced back through the needle.

Centrifuge

A machine that spins blood samples at high speed to separate blood components.

Positive Reinforcement

The use of rewards, like treats, to encourage good behavior in a patient during and after procedures.

Restraint

Methods used to safely and comfortably hold an animal during a procedure, ensuring safety for both the animal and personnel.

modules.content:
Before we get started, let’s review a few key terms we’ll go over in the upcoming section on urine collection.

Key terms

Cystocentesis & Free Catch Urine Key Terms

Two urine collection methods follow: cystocentesis, which is sterile and ultrasound-guided, and free catch, which is clean but not sterile.

Cystocentesis

A procedure where a needle is inserted through the abdominal wall into the bladder to collect a sterile urine sample.

Dorsal recumbency

A position where the animal lies on its back with legs extended, preferred for performing a cystocentesis.

Ultrasound

A non-invasive imaging technique using sound waves to create images of internal organs, used to visualize the bladder during cystocentesis.

Sterile technique

Maintaining sterility during cystocentesis to prevent contamination, using gloves, sterile needles, and alcohol to clean the skin and collection tube.

Voided sample / free catch

A urine sample collected as the animal urinates naturally, using a ladle or clean container.

Midstream sample

Collecting a urine sample by allowing some urine to pass initially before collecting to reduce contamination risk.

Choosing a method

Cystocentesis produces a sterile sample suitable for culture. A voided or free catch sample is appropriate when a sterile sample is not required, and a midstream collection reduces the risk of contamination.

modules.content:

Cystocentesis

Feline cystocentesis performed with ultrasound guidance. The source document labels this screen “Cystocentis”; the correct spelling is used here.

Key points

  • Dorsal recumbency is the preferred position.
  • Sterile preparation of the site is essential.
  • The ultrasound probe visualizes the bladder and guides needle insertion.
  • Transfer the urine to a sterile tube using a new needle to maintain sterility.

Before we get started, let’s review a few key terms we’ll go over in the upcoming section on ear swabs.

Key terms

Ear Swab Key Terms

Ear Swab Cytology

The process of collecting a sample from the ear canal using a cotton-tipped applicator.

Mineral Oil

A clear, odorless oil used with a microscope slide to examine the ear swab sample for ear mites.

Microscope Slide

A thin, flat piece of glass used to hold specimens for examination under a microscope.

Ear Mites

Tiny parasitic mites that infest ear canals, causing irritation, inflammation, and dark, waxy debris.

Staining

A technique used to enhance the visibility of cells and microorganisms under a microscope.

Debris

Material collected from the ear canal during swabbing, including wax, dead skin cells, hair, and microorganisms.

Frosted Edge

A rough, frosted section on one end of the microscope slide, positioned at the top.

Rolling Technique

A gentle rolling motion when applying the ear swab sample to the microscope slide.

modules.content:
Clinical Techniques I: Needles, Syringes & Handling Sharps. Expand each of the eight sections below. Each section opens and closes independently, so you can compare two topics side by side.

Interactive

Needles, Syringes & Handling Sharps

Every section is keyboard accessible: move to a heading with Tab, then press Enter or Space to open and close it.

1. Needle Gauges+
  • Larger gauge numbers indicate smaller needle diameters.
  • Common gauges include 25G (red), 22G (blue), 20G (pink), and 18G (green).
  • Needle lengths vary from 5/8 inch to 2 inches.
2. Syringes+
  • Syringes are measured in cc or mL, with common sizes being 1 cc, 3 cc, 6 cc, 12 cc, 20 cc, 35 cc, and 60 cc.
  • Insulin syringes are measured in units.
  • Types of tips include Luer lock, Luer slip, and catheter tip.
3. Medication Withdrawal+
  1. Wash hands and gather supplies.
  2. Choose the appropriate syringe and needle size.
  3. Clean the top of the medication vial with alcohol.
  4. Draw air into the syringe equal to the desired medication volume.
  5. Insert the needle into the vial and inject the air.
  6. Withdraw the desired amount of medication.
  7. Expel any air bubbles.
  8. Recap the needle using a one-handed technique.

Always check the medication label for correct dosage, concentration, and expiration date.

4. Identify Sharps+
  • Recognize items like needles, scalpel blades, and broken glass as potential hazards.
5. Safe Handling Practices+
  • Avoid recapping needles. If necessary, use a one-handed technique.
  • Never break or bend needles.
  • Do not pick up broken glass with bare hands; use tongs or a broom.
6. Sharps Container Use+
  • Use puncture-resistant, leak-proof containers.
  • Place containers in areas where sharps are generated.
  • Keep containers upright and avoid overfilling.
  • Seal containers securely when full.
  • Never reach into a sharps container; use a tool to push down contents.
7. Injury Prevention+
  • Immediately report any needle stick injuries to your supervisor.
  • Thoroughly clean the affected area with soap and water.
8. Regulatory Compliance+
  • Follow OSHA guidelines for sharps handling and disposal.
  • Ensure proper labeling and color-coding of sharps containers.
  • By following these guidelines, you can significantly reduce the risk of injury and promote a safer work environment.

modules.content:
Source order: screen 25

Blood Collection Tubes

Watch the Tubes demonstration, then use the reference below to review tube selection and safe sample transfer.

Reference

Tube selection at a glance

Know which tests are ordered before you begin so the correct tubes are drawn the first time and the patient does not need a second blood draw. Label every tube with the patient’s full name and the date.

Red top

Additive
No additive, or a serum separator
Used for
Serum chemistry and serology
Handling
Allow the sample to sit and clot before centrifuging.

Purple top

Additive
EDTA
Used for
Hematology (CBC)
Handling
Place on a rocker to mix the anticoagulant gently and completely.

Green top

Additive
Lithium heparin
Used for
Plasma chemistry
Handling
Invert gently to mix; do not shake.

Blue top

Additive
Sodium citrate
Used for
Coagulation studies
Handling
Fill to the marked volume — the additive-to-blood ratio matters.

White top

Additive
Varies by manufacturer
Used for
General purpose, including urine samples
Handling
Confirm the intended use with the laboratory before collecting.

Filling tubes safely

  • Remove the needle from the syringe before transferring blood to the tubes.
  • Remove the tube caps and insert the blood directly into the tube — never force blood back through a needle.
  • Gently mix tubes containing anticoagulants so the additive is distributed through the sample.
  • Forcing blood through a needle is the most common preventable cause of hemolysis.

modules.title: Course Recap
modules.completionHeading: Read the fifteen recap points, then mark this module complete.
modules.completionBody: Mark this module complete when you have worked through the content above. Your progress is recorded and you can reopen the module at any time.
modules.content:
Let’s do a recap of the key points we covered in this course. All fifteen points below come directly from the source course recap.

Recap

Fifteen key points

Read through the full list before starting the final assessment. Every assessment question is drawn from this material.

  1. 1

    Initial Preparation

    Understand the specific tests required before beginning any procedure to ensure the correct tubes are used, avoiding the need for additional blood draws. Label the tubes properly with the patient's full name and the date to prevent mix-ups.

  2. 2

    Jugular Venipuncture

    For canine patients, the dog should be in a sitting position if possible. If this is uncomfortable, standing is acceptable, as long as the dog cannot back out of the position. The restrainer's hands should be placed to occlude the vessel and provide support but also be out of the way of the needle.

  3. 3

    Lateral Saphenous Venipuncture

    Again, for a canine patient, a standing position is easiest, although smaller dogs can be held off the table as long as they are secure and unable to bite. The restrainer will apply pressure to the back of the leg to occlude the vessel. This vein is good for quick, simple blood draws and for dogs that are aggressive or difficult to handle at the front end.

  4. 4

    Cephalic Venipuncture

    For canine patients, the dog can be in any position that is comfortable for the patient, the restrainer, and the person performing the venipuncture. When drawing blood, the restrainer will roll the chosen leg off and hold behind the elbow so the dog can't pull back.

  5. 5

    Site Preparation

    Clean the area with isopropyl alcohol to wet the fur, separate it, and provide visualization of the vein.

  6. 6

    Equipment

    A 3 cc syringe with a 22-gauge needle is commonly used. The appropriate blood tubes are necessary, and the type of tube depends on the tests ordered. Red top tubes (with or without a serum separator) for serum, purple top tubes with EDTA for hematology, green top tubes with lithium heparin for plasma, blue top tubes with sodium citrate for coagulation studies, and white top tubes, which can be used for a variety of purposes, including urine samples.

  7. 7

    Venipuncture Technique

    Ensure the needle bevel is facing up and is parallel to the skin. Insert the needle slowly and gently until a flashback of blood is seen in the hub of the needle. Pull back slowly on the plunger, collecting the required volume of blood.

  8. 8

    Post-Venipuncture Care

    Apply pressure to the site immediately after removing the needle. Gauze can be used for this, and then a Vet Wrap can be applied to maintain pressure, ensuring it is not too tight. Give the patient positive reinforcement, such as a treat, to create a positive association with the procedure.

  9. 9

    Sample Handling

    Remove the needle from the syringe before transferring blood to tubes to prevent hemolysis. Remove the caps from blood tubes and insert the blood directly into the tube to avoid forcing the blood back through the needle. Gently mix tubes containing anticoagulants to ensure proper mixing of the anticoagulant with the blood. Follow specific instructions for different types of tubes, such as placing purple top tubes on a rocker and allowing red top tubes to sit and clot before centrifuging.

  10. 10

    Cystocentesis

    This method uses ultrasound guidance to collect urine directly from the bladder and is considered a sterile technique. Dorsal recumbency is the preferred position. Sterile preparation of the site is essential. The ultrasound probe is used to visualize the bladder and guide the needle insertion. Once the urine is collected, transfer it to a sterile urine tube using a new needle to maintain sterility.

  11. 11

    Voided Urine Sample

    This method involves collecting urine as the dog urinates, aiming for a midstream sample. Cleanliness, though not sterility, is important. A ladle or clean container is used to collect the urine, which is then transferred to a syringe.

  12. 12

    Clipping

    Clipping the fur at the venipuncture site may be necessary, particularly for dogs with thick coats, to improve visualization of the vein and maintain cleanliness.

  13. 13

    Gloves

    Wearing gloves is essential to maintain hygiene and prevent the transfer of contaminants.

  14. 14

    Patient Comfort and Stress Monitoring

    Using positive reinforcement and gentle handling techniques is crucial. If a patient becomes overly stressed, sedation may be considered.

  15. 15

    Safety

    It is important to remember that working with animals always involves inherent risks. Proper restraint techniques and awareness of potential hazards are crucial to ensuring the safety of both the handler and the animal.

modules.title: Final Assessment
modules.content:
End-of-course assessment. Five questions, drawn from the blood collection, sample handling, and cystocentesis material you have just completed. Each question is scored as soon as you answer it, and a score of 75% or higher marks this module — and the lesson — complete.

Before you begin

How this assessment is scored

Select one answer per question. Feedback appears immediately, and your overall score is recorded in your Hannah Learning System progress once all five questions are answered.

Course completion

Finishing this assessment completes the Sample Collection lesson. The source course ends with a celebratory completion animation; that asset has not been approved for this build, so the lesson closes with your recorded score and a return to the Clinical Diagnostics curriculum.

quiz.q: Which of the following blood collection tubes contains an anticoagulant that prevents clotting and is typically used for hematology studies?
opts: Red top tube
Purple top tube
Green top tube
Blue top tube
quiz.exp: Purple top tubes contain EDTA, the anticoagulant used for hematology studies such as a CBC. Red tops have no anticoagulant, green tops use lithium heparin for plasma, and blue tops use sodium citrate for coagulation studies.

quiz.q: When performing a lateral saphenous venipuncture, what is the primary method of occluding the vein?
opts: Applying a tourniquet above the venipuncture site
Applying pressure to the back of the leg
Elevating the leg above the heart
Using a specialized clamp
quiz.exp: The restrainer applies pressure to the back of the leg to occlude the lateral saphenous vein, which makes it more prominent for the draw.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove the needle from the syringe before transferring blood into collection tubes?
opts: To ensure the correct volume of blood is collected
To prevent contamination of the sample
To minimize the risk of hemolysis
To facilitate mixing of the blood with additives in the tube
quiz.exp: Forcing blood back through a needle ruptures red blood cells. Removing the needle and inserting the blood directly into an uncapped tube minimizes hemolysis.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of using the lateral saphenous vein for blood collection?
opts: It allows for collection of large blood volumes.
It is a suitable option for quick and simple blood draws.
It is easily accessible in all animal species.
It minimizes patient discomfort.
quiz.exp: The lateral saphenous vein is well suited to quick, simple blood draws, and it lets the team work away from the front end of a dog that is aggressive or difficult to handle.

quiz.q: During a cystocentesis, what instrument is used to guide the needle into the bladder?
opts: X-ray machine
Ultrasound
Stethoscope
Otoscope
quiz.exp: Ultrasound is used to visualize the bladder and guide needle insertion during a cystocentesis.
